content: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a member of the herpesvirus family and is one of the most common human viruses. It primarily targets the oropharyngeal epithelium and B lymphocytes. Transmission of EBV through air or blood is uncommon. The incubation period, which is the time from infection to the onset of symptoms, typically ranges from 4 to 6 weeks. Individuals with infectious mononucleosis can spread the virus to others for several weeks, but no special isolation precautions are recommended because the virus is frequently found in the saliva of healthy individuals. Many healthy people can intermittently carry and spread the virus for life, serving as the primary reservoir for person-to-person transmission. Consequently, preventing the transmission of EBV is nearly impossible. The majority of mononucleosis cases are caused by EBV, and most individuals become infected with the virus at some point in their lives. It is estimated that 90-95% of people over the age of 21 have antibodies to EBV. In the United States, the disease is most common among older children and young adults. However, in socioeconomically disadvantaged areas, young children are often infected and remain asymptomatic. The virus's dormant nature and the long incubation period make epidemiological control of the disease impractical. Most people are infected with EBV during their lifetime, with 90-95% of adults showing seropositivity by the age of 21. Even individuals exposed to infected contacts are often already seropositive and therefore not at risk of developing mononucleosis. Once infected, the virus remains in the body for life, typically residing dormant in B lymphocytes. Reactivation of the virus can occur periodically, during which the individual may become infectious again, though usually without symptoms. In susceptible hosts, reactivation under certain environmental stressors may cause vague subclinical symptoms or remain asymptomatic, detectable only through serologic testing. During this phase, the virus can still spread to others. EBV is a ubiquitous virus worldwide and is the primary causative agent of infectious mononucleosis. Initial exposure to the virus often occurs during or after adolescence. While historically referred to as The Kissing Disease, recent research indicates that transmission can occur not only through intimate contact with infected saliva but also through airborne exposure to the virus. Acute mononucleosis, acute cytomegalovirus infection, and Toxoplasma gondii infection share similar clinical presentations. Since their management is often similar, distinguishing between infectious mononucleosis and cytomegalovirus infection is not always necessary. However, in pregnant women, differentiating mononucleosis from toxoplasmosis is critical due to the significant consequences of toxoplasmosis for the fetus. Acute HIV infection can also mimic the symptoms of infectious mononucleosis, and testing should be performed in pregnant women for the same reasons as toxoplasmosis. Fatalities from mononucleosis are extremely rare in developed nations. However, chronic subclinical infection may persist due to the dormant virus within B cells. Reactivation of the virus can occur in susceptible hosts under appropriate environmental stressors. Such reactivation or chronic subclinical viral activity may trigger autoimmune diseases and cancers due to the virus's predilection for B lymphocytes and its ability to alter lymphocyte proliferation and antibody production. The symptoms of infectious mononucleosis include fever, sore throat, and swollen lymph glands. Splenomegaly or hepatomegaly may also develop in some cases. Heart problems or central nervous system involvement are rare, and the disease is almost never fatal. There are no known associations between active EBV infection and pregnancy complications, such as miscarriages or birth defects. While symptoms typically resolve within 1 to 2 months, EBV remains dormant in a few cells in the throat and blood for the rest of the individual's life. Periodic reactivation of the virus can occur, often without symptoms, and the virus is commonly found in the saliva of infected individuals during these episodes. The classic initial presentation of mononucleosis includes fever, lymphadenopathy, pharyngitis, rash, and/or periorbital edema. Occasionally, patients may also exhibit splenomegaly, which can lead to life-threatening complications such as splenic rupture, and/or hepatomegaly. In most cases, the clinical diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis can be made based on the characteristic triad of fever, pharyngitis, and lymphadenopathy lasting 1 to 4 weeks. Persistent viral infection has been observed in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome, possibly due to microglial activation during the acute infection phase. Lumbar puncture, EEG, CT scan, or MRI may be used to evaluate patients with presumed central nervous system involvement. Bilateral tender lymphadenopathy, particularly in the posterior cervical lymph nodes, is characteristic of mononucleosis. Lymph node biopsy, if performed, may reveal atypical lymphocytosis. Infectious mononucleosis is generally self-limiting, and treatment is primarily symptomatic and supportive. Severe tonsillar enlargement may cause life-threatening airway obstruction, necessitating close monitoring of high-risk patients. Glucocorticoids may be indicated in cases of severe airway obstruction. Antiviral agents such as acyclovir have been used to reduce oropharyngeal viral shedding. Recently, valacyclovir has been shown to lower or eliminate the presence of EBV in patients with acute mononucleosis, significantly reducing symptom severity. Surgical intervention is rarely required for infectious mononucleosis. However, in cases of life-threatening splenic rupture, which can occur even without trauma, immediate surgery may be life-saving. The majority of mononucleosis cases are caused by EBV, and most individuals become infected with the virus at some point in their lives. Transmission requires intimate contact with the saliva of an infected person and rarely occurs via air or blood. Therefore, the most effective way to prevent mononucleosis is to avoid close contact with infected saliva.
